name: Republic of Haiti
info: The republic restored in 1859 after Soulouque's empire, heir of the only state born of a slave revolt, marked since by debt to France, US occupation, the Duvalier dictatorship and today's collapse of the state.

facts.founder: Fabre Geffrard, who overthrew Emperor Faustin Soulouque and became president in January 1859
facts.predecessor: Independent Haiti of 1804: Dessalines's empire, the Kingdom of Haiti and the republic of Pétion and Boyer, then the Second Empire of Faustin Soulouque (1849–1859)

t: Haiti, independent since 1 January 1804 as the only state established by a slave revolt, paid France 150 million francs (reduced to 90 million in 1838) for recognition; by 1900 debt repayment took 80% of government spending, and the debt was not cleared until 1947.

US Marines occupied Haiti from July 1915 to 1934, imposing a constitution that allowed foreign land ownership and building roads by forced labour; the Duvaliers (1957–1986) ruled by terror through the Tontons Macoutes, killing an estimated 40,000 to 60,000 people.

The earthquake of 12 January 2010 killed between 160,000 and 316,000 people; since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse on 7 July 2021 the presidency has been vacant, gangs control most of Port-au-Prince and no elected official remains.
dyk: The constitution written for Haiti under US occupation in 1915, which for the first time allowed foreigners to own land in the country, was drafted by the future US president Franklin D. Roosevelt.
ev: On 15 January Emperor Faustin Soulouque abdicates after General Fabre Geffrard's revolution and the republic is restored, with Geffrard as president.
After President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam's execution of 167 prisoners and his lynching, US Marines land at Port-au-Prince; the occupation lasts until 1934.
Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo's army bludgeons and bayonets 20,000–30,000 Haitians on the border in the Parsley Massacre.
François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier is elected president; he rules by terror until his death in 1971 and is followed by his son until 1986.
Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier leaves the country under US pressure after nationwide demonstrations.
Operation Uphold Democracy: 20,000 US troops enter Haiti and Jean-Bertrand Aristide, overthrown by Raoul Cédras's coup of 1991, is restored.
On 12 January a magnitude-7.0 earthquake kills between 160,000 and 316,000 people and leaves up to 1.6 million homeless; a cholera outbreak from a UN base follows.
On 7 July President Jovenel Moïse is assassinated at his residence; the presidency has remained vacant and the state has since collapsed.

sections.foundation:
Haiti, the Taíno name for Hispaniola, was reclaimed in 1804 by Jean-Jacques Dessalines for the state the enslaved people of French Saint-Domingue had won. The revolution begun in August 1791 under Toussaint Louverture, the abolition of slavery in 1793 and Napoleon's expedition of 1802, ended at the Battle of Vertières on 18 November 1803 and in the declaration of independence of 1 January 1804: the first state in the Americas to abolish slavery and the only one established by a slave revolt. Dessalines, Emperor Jacques I, had 3,000 to 5,000 remaining whites killed and was assassinated in 1806; Henri Christophe's northern kingdom and Alexandre Pétion's southern republic were reunited by Jean-Pierre Boyer in 1820, who conquered Santo Domingo in 1822.

In 1825, under the guns of a French fleet, Boyer bought recognition for 150 million francs. He fell in 1843, the Dominicans broke away on 27 February 1844, and Haiti's armies failed to retake the east in 1845 and 1849; General Faustin Soulouque, president from 1847, made himself emperor and launched the campaigns of 1849 and 1855. Their losses and sacrifices without result provoked a revolution led by General Fabre Geffrard in 1858, who defeated the army and took most of the country in December. Soulouque abdicated on 15 January 1859 and went into exile, and Geffrard became president of the restored republic.
sections.socioeconomy:
Haiti occupies the mountainous western three-eighths of Hispaniola, 27,750 square kilometres, and with about 11.4 million people is the most populous country in the Caribbean. Nearly all speak Haitian Creole, French the educated 42%; 55% were Catholic and 29% Protestant in 2018, while 50–80% keep some element of Vodou, recognised by the state in 2003. The colonial order survived as a social one: the mulatto elite, 5% of the population, has kept its pre-eminence in politics, economy and culture. Haiti is the only country in the Americas classified as least developed: three-quarters of its people live on US$2 or less a day, 30% in extreme poverty in 2021, the informal economy gives 90% of employment, and 75% of households lack running water.

Agriculture employs 40–50% of Haitians; coffee, mangoes, cacao and vetiver, of which Haiti grows half the world's supply for perfume, are exported, but the country imports half its food and 80% of its rice. Remittances from the diaspora in the United States, Canada, France and the Dominican Republic equal a fifth of GDP, five times export earnings, and by 2004 four in five Haitian graduates lived abroad. Aid has flowed since 1990, more than US$4 billion by 2003 and US$13.34 billion earmarked after the 2010 earthquake, with mixed results: the Caracol industrial park opened in 2012 with 65,000 promised jobs had created 5,000 and displaced 3,500 farmers a decade later.
sections.military:
The Haitian army inherited the glory of 1803, but in the republic it made and broke presidents: Haiti has suffered 32 coups since independence. In July 1915, after President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam executed 167 political prisoners and was lynched, Woodrow Wilson sent in the Marines; they took the capital, its banks and customs house within days. The Cacos under Charlemagne Péralte fought them until his capture and execution in 1919, and the Marine commandant counted 2,250 or 3,250 Haitians killed in twenty months of unrest. The occupation ended in 1934.

In 1937 Dominican troops under Rafael Trujillo killed 20,000–30,000 Haitians on the border in the Parsley Massacre. François Duvalier, distrusting an army he purged repeatedly, built the Tontons Macoutes, a private militia that terrorised the population; the 1964 rising at Jérémie was crushed with public executions. The army overthrew Jean-Bertrand Aristide in September 1991 under Raoul Cédras, and in September 1994 20,000 US troops under Operation Uphold Democracy restored him. The Armed Forces were disbanded in 1995, a National Police took their place, and the army was reconstituted only in 2017, some 2,000 strong by 2023. Since 2020 the state has lost its monopoly of force: gangs held about 80% of Port-au-Prince by late 2023, killed 4,789 people and kidnapped 2,490 that year, and neither the police, bled by desertion, nor the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support Mission has restored public safety.
sections.governance:
The republic of 1859 was presidential and unstable. Under the US occupation (1915–1934) a client president was installed within weeks and a constitution drafted by Franklin D. Roosevelt permitted foreign ownership of land for the first time; an American financial adviser ran the budget until 1941. François Duvalier, elected in September 1957, proclaimed himself President for Life in 1964 and ruled through the Tontons Macoutes; his son Jean-Claude succeeded him in 1971 and fled in February 1986. Some 40,000 to 60,000 Haitians were killed under the two Duvaliers.

The Constitution of 1987, amended in 2012, made a semi-presidential republic: a president elected for five years without consecutive terms, a prime minister from the majority in the National Assembly, a two-chamber National Assembly and a modified Napoleonic Code. It has rarely worked as written. Elections in 1987 were aborted by shootings, those of 1988 drew 4% of voters, Aristide was elected in 1990 and overthrown in 1991, re-elected in 2000 with 92% on an opposition boycott and driven out in 2004; Michel Martelly left in 2016 without a successor, Jovenel Moïse won on a 17% turnout and was assassinated in 2021. Since 2023 no elected official remains: a Transitional Presidential Council governed from 25 April 2024 until its mandate expired on 7 February 2026, leaving acting prime minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé as sole executive with elections postponed indefinitely.
sections.impact:
Haiti's weight in history is out of all proportion to its size. Its revolution ended slavery in the richest plantation colony on earth, defeated Napoleon, who then sold Louisiana and so frightened the slave-holding United States that recognition waited until 1862. Pétion's republic gave Simón Bolívar the arms and money that let him liberate New Granada, and Haiti ruled the whole island from 1822 to 1844, ending slavery in Santo Domingo. The ransom paid to France, estimated to have cost between $21 billion and $115 billion in lost growth, made Haiti the first post-colonial state crippled by debt; in 2013 its government called on European governments to pay reparations for slavery.

The republic was a founding member of the League of Nations and, on 27 September 1945, of the United Nations. Its diaspora in the United States, the Dominican Republic and Cuba carried its culture abroad. Haitian Creole, official beside French, has had a literature of its own since Franketienne's Dezafi (1975), and writers from Jacques Roumain to Edwidge Danticat and Dany Laferrière and the music of compas and Rara are known across the world. The Citadelle Laferrière, the largest fortress in the Americas, and the Sans-Souci Palace were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982. Haiti's disasters have also shaped the world's institutions: the UN's cholera, brought in 2010 by its own peacekeepers and killing some 10,000, drew an apology in 2016 but no admission of fault.
sections.decline:
Haiti's recent decades have been a descent. After the Duvaliers' flight in 1986 came aborted and fraudulent elections, Aristide's election and overthrow in 1990–91, his restoration by US troops in 1994, the contested election of 2000 and the revolt that forced him out again in 2004. Then nature struck a broken state: on 12 January 2010 a magnitude-7.0 earthquake killed between 160,000 and 316,000 people and left up to 1.6 million homeless; cholera from a UN base then killed some 10,000. Hurricane Matthew delayed the elections of 2016, won on a 17% turnout by Jovenel Moïse.

Protests against fuel prices from July 2018 became demands for Moïse's resignation; on 7 July 2021 he was assassinated at his residence, and a second great earthquake struck on 14 August. By March 2022 Haiti had no president, no parliamentary quorum and no working high court, and the gang war begun in 2020 has consumed the country: armed groups held an estimated 80% of the capital by late 2023, killed 4,789 people, kidnapped 2,490 and displaced 362,000 that year; over 2.7 million live under gang control and more than 1.3 million have been displaced, and in March 2024 nearly half the population faced acute food insecurity. Ariel Henry, kept out of the country by gangs, resigned; the Transitional Presidential Council ruled from 25 April 2024 to 7 February 2026 without an election. With no elected official left, Haiti has been described as a failed state in virtual anarchy.

summary: The Republic of Haiti, restored in 1859 after Soulouque's empire, inherited the pride and the debts of the only nation born of a slave revolt. Coups, the US occupation of 1915–1934, the Duvalier terror and the earthquake of 2010 wore down the state, and since the assassination of President Moïse in 2021 gangs rule most of the capital and no elected official remains.
references: Robert Heinl, Written in Blood: The History of the Haitian People (University Press of America, 1996)
Helen Chapin Metz, Dominican Republic and Haiti: Country Studies (Federal Research Division, Library of Congress, 2001)
Philippe Girard, Haiti: The Tumultuous History (Palgrave, 2010)
C. L. R. James, The Black Jacobins: Toussaint l'Ouverture and the San Domingo Revolution (Secker & Warburg, 1938)
Colin Dayan, Haiti, History, and the Gods (University of California Press, 1998)
Amy Wilentz, The Rainy Season: Haiti Since Duvalier (Simon & Schuster, 1990)

pointDescs.1859: Soulouque abdicates on 15 January after Fabre Geffrard's revolution; Geffrard becomes president of the restored republic.
pointDescs.1867: Geffrard is overthrown in a coup, as his successor Sylvain Salnave is in 1869: the turbulent decades after the empire begin.
pointDescs.1879: Lysius Salomon's presidency (1879–1888) and Florvil Hyppolite's (1889–1896) bring some modernisation of the economy and infrastructure; Hyppolite refuses the United States a naval base at Môle Saint-Nicolas in 1889.
pointDescs.1900: Debt repayment to France consumes 80% of government spending; Germany has already humiliated the government in the Lüders affair of 1897, and short presidencies follow.
pointDescs.1915: After President Sam's execution of 167 prisoners and his lynching, US Marines occupy the country, install a client president and impose a constitution allowing foreign land ownership; the Cacos resist until 1919.
pointDescs.1934: The occupation ends under President Sténio Vincent, leaving 1,700 km of usable roads, 189 bridges and a centralised state; a US financial adviser keeps the budget until 1941.
pointDescs.1950: Paul Magloire takes power with US backing; the French debt was finally paid off in 1947, Haiti is a founding member of the United Nations (1945), and stability brings the first tourists to a redeveloped Port-au-Prince waterfront.
pointDescs.1957: François Duvalier is elected in September; initially popular, he builds the Tontons Macoutes and purges the army.
pointDescs.1964: Duvalier proclaims himself President for Life and crushes the rising at Jérémie; the educated class begins to leave the country.
pointDescs.1986: Jean-Claude Duvalier flees in February after demonstrations spread from Gonaïves; 40,000 to 60,000 have died under the two Duvaliers.
pointDescs.1991: Jean-Bertrand Aristide, elected in 1990, is overthrown by the military under Raoul Cédras in September; many Haitians try to flee.
pointDescs.1994: Operation Uphold Democracy brings 20,000 US troops and restores Aristide in October; the army is disbanded in 1995 and a National Police created.
pointDescs.2004: A revolt from the north forces Aristide into exile; MINUSTAH arrives; Tropical Storm Jeanne kills 3,006.
pointDescs.2010: The earthquake of 12 January kills between 160,000 and 316,000 and makes up to 1.6 million homeless; cholera from a UN base kills some 10,000 more. GDP falls 8%.
pointDescs.2017: Jovenel Moïse is sworn in as 48th president after elections on a 17% turnout; the army is reconstituted.
pointDescs.2021: Moïse is assassinated on 7 July; a second great earthquake follows on 14 August, and the gang war becomes general.
pointDescs.2025: No elected official remains; gangs control most of the capital, over 1.3 million are displaced, and the transitional council's mandate expires in February 2026 without an election.

notes: The register starts this state in 1859 (the return of the republic after Soulouque's empire); the revolution, Dessalines, Christophe, Pétion, Boyer and Soulouque are in 'foundation' and the predecessor fact, as instructed.
The founder fact names Geffrard as the restorer of the republic; the article names no founder of the 1859 republic as such.
The article gives both 2,250 and 3,250 Haitians killed under the occupation (two reports by the Marine commandant); both given.
Historical influence stat (6) rests on the revolution's impact, which the article describes at length though it predates the register's start year.
Peak set at 1950 (Magloire's stability, debt paid in 1947, UN founding membership): a judgement; the article does not say when Haiti was strongest.
References: the article's Sources and Further reading sections; Heinl, Metz, Girard, James, Dayan and Wilentz chosen as general histories.
